    {
      "startEvent": 664,
      "endEvent": 668,
      "contextStartEvent": 590,
      "contextEndEvent": 684,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "history tends to be written by the victors. And so history is always suspect.",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "no",
      "emotionalDevices": ["none"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The familiar maxim helps move from reports to generalized historical suspicion without establishing victor control of these sources (E664–668). However, it accompanies reasons concerning testing and source limitations (E590–662), and 'suspect' need not mean rejected. Whether it replaces an inference or simply summarizes methodological caution remains uncertain."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 876,
      "endEvent": 879,
      "contextStartEvent": 827,
      "contextEndEvent": 910,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "The only reason this feels reasonable to people is because they've already accepted other things that aren't reasonable to accept.",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["none"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The exclusive psychological explanation could preempt believers' reasons by treating their judgment as inherited irrationality. No evidence establishes that exclusive cause. Yet B supplies evidential objections (E879–890), earlier labels his motivational account speculation (E853–868), and does not explicitly reject every possible objection because of the believer's defect."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2565,
      "endEvent": 2582,
      "contextStartEvent": 2547,
      "contextEndEvent": 2617,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "they really, really get mad because I'm willing to say I don't know",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "yes",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": ["ridicule", "shame"],
      "confidence": "high",
      "explanation": "B answers the accusation of dodging partly by attributing critics' anger to discomfort with uncertainty and contrasting it with religious arrogance (E2565–2582). That motive is not demonstrated and discredits this criticism independently of its merits. Fairly, he also directly answers that he has discussed fallacies and evidence (E2559–2564)."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2633,
      "endEvent": 2659,
      "contextStartEvent": 2618,
      "contextEndEvent": 2679,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "All we need to say is, well, does God have good reasons for revealing himself in the way he does?",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["none"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Invoking God's reasons and excessively high evidential bars could insulate the timing of revelation from criticism (E2633–2656). However, A gives specific tradeoffs involving earlier populations, writing, and roads (E2638–2647), then requests evaluation of existing evidence. The passage does not clearly authorize unlimited unseen reasons against every contrary pattern."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 3631,
      "endEvent": 3645,
      "contextStartEvent": 3625,
      "contextEndEvent": 3671,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "Which means the only option that you're left for is that Matt's a big fat liar",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "yes",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": ["ridicule"],
      "confidence": "high",
      "explanation": "B converts God's ability to provide unmistakable evidence into certainty that he has not missed sufficient evidence, leaving critics only an accusation of lying (E3631–3645). The missing step connects possible divine persuasion to actual recognition. His qualification 'if he wants me to know' narrows the theology but does not earn that exclusive alternative."
    }
  ],

    {

      "quote": "coincidences are God's attempt at humor.",
      "explanation": "A treats the saying lightly, questions its attribution, and immediately explains that billions of people make unusual coincidences expected. He explicitly denies that such coincidences provide strong evidence for God (E2775–2784)."
    },

      "quote": "extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.",
